related_flag_targets.statement:
Problem 2

(Suggested by Allen Knutson) Let me motivate this by stating a theorem of Brion. Suppose you have a variety X lying in a flag manifold G/P. We say that X is multiplicity-free if in cohomology [X] =

∑

> S⊂W/WP

[Xs],

i.e. each zero-dimensional intersection with a general translate of a Schubert variety is empty or 1 point.

Theorem 2.1 (Brion). If X is multiplicity-free, then X degenerates to the reduced union of Schubert varieties (as predicted by S ), and this union is Cohen-Macaulay.

In particular, if X is reduced and irreducible and multiplicity-free, then X is Cohen-Macaulay.

prior_report.problem:
The canonical record is item 2 in the problem-session notes for the AIM workshop *Degenerations in Algebraic Geometry*, suggested by Allen Knutson. The source is the six-page PDF dated September 7, 2016.

The OCR in the canonical JSON damaged the displayed summation. Inspection of page 2 of the PDF gives the intended notation
\[
 [X]=\sum_{s\in S}[X_s],\qquad S\subset W/W_P.
\]
With that repair, the record says:

> Let \(X\) be a variety in a flag manifold \(G/P\). It is multiplicity-free if its cohomology class is a sum of distinct Schubert classes, equivalently if every zero-dimensional intersection with a general translate of a complementary Schubert variety is empty or one point. Brion's theorem says that \(X\) degenerates to the corresponding reduced union of Schubert varieties and that this union is Cohen--Macaulay. In particular, a reduced irreducible multiplicity-free \(X\) is Cohen--Macaulay.

The source layout matters. The text above ends with the Cohen--Macaulay corollary. A new, separately numbered paragraph then begins “Problem 2.2” and asks a classification question. Thus the present canonical record, AIM-ALGEBRAIC_GEOMETRY-0217, is a contextual theorem statement and contains no unresolved question of its own. The appropriate status is therefore `context_only`. This report does not claim to solve or classify the subsets asked about in the separately indexed Problem 2.2.
prior_report.status_literature:
Brion's original theorem is stronger than the workshop paraphrase. Over an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic, an integral multiplicity-free subvariety \(V\) of a flag variety is normal and Cohen--Macaulay and has a flat degeneration, inside the flag variety, to a reduced Cohen--Macaulay union of Schubert varieties. Brion also proves restriction-surjectivity and cohomology vanishing for globally generated line bundles, and arithmetic normality and arithmetic Cohen--Macaulayness for embeddings defined by ample line bundles [Brion 2003].

The proof uses the Chow variety and Borel's fixed-point theorem to specialize \(V\) to a \(B\)-fixed cycle. Multiplicity-freeness makes that cycle a sum of distinct Schubert cycles. Brion proves that the total space is normal and Cohen--Macaulay; the special fiber is equidimensional, Cohen--Macaulay, and generically reduced, hence reduced. This verifies the mathematical content of the AIM record. Brion's theorem is established, not open.

Later work supplies a useful combinatorial description in products of projective spaces. Castillo, Cid-Ruiz, Li, Montaño, and Zhang prove that the support of the multidegrees of an irreducible multiprojective variety is a discrete algebraic polymatroid and characterize positivity by dimensions of all coordinate projections [Castillo et al. 2020, Theorem 3.12]. When every factor is \(\mathbb P^1\), this support is the set of bases of a matroid. Ardila and Boocher give a large explicit family: closures of linear spaces in \((\mathbb P^1)^n\), whose multidegrees and Cohen--Macaulay degenerations are governed by a linear matroid [Ardila--Boocher 2016]. Eur and Larson use Brion's degeneration in a modern matroidal treatment of \(K\)-theoretic positivity; in particular, they record that the \(K\)-class of an irreducible multiplicity-free subvariety of a product of projective spaces is controlled by its projection polymatroid [Eur--Larson 2026].

The contribution developed below is not a new proof of Brion's theorem. It extracts additional function-field structure from the multiplicity-one condition in the first test geometry \((\mathbb P^1)^n\).
prior_report.work_done:
### 3. Definitions and assumptions

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic and let
\[
 X\subseteq Y=(\mathbb P^1_k)^n
\]
be an integral closed subvariety of dimension \(d\geq 1\). Let \(h_i\) denote the pullback of the hyperplane class from the \(i\)-th factor. Since \(h_i^2=0\), there are uniquely determined nonnegative integers \(m_B\), indexed by \(d\)-element subsets \(B\subseteq[n]\), such that
\[
 [X]=\sum_{\substack{B\subseteq[n]\\ |B|=d}}
 m_B\prod_{i\notin B}h_i .
\]
Equivalently,
\[
 m_B=\deg\left([X]\cdot\prod_{i\in B}h_i\right).
\]
The variety \(X\) is multiplicity-free precisely when every \(m_B\) is \(0\) or \(1\).

Choose an affine coordinate on each \(\mathbb P^1\) whose pole does not contain the generic point of \(X\), and denote its restriction to \(X\) by \(t_i\in K:=k(X)\). Factorwise changes of affine coordinate act by \(\operatorname{PGL}_2(k)\) and do not change the subfields generated by the \(t_i\). Define
\[
 r(I)=\operatorname{trdeg}_k k(t_i:i\in I),\qquad I\subseteq[n].
\]
The coordinate functions generate \(K\), so \(r([n])=d\). The function \(r\) is the rank function of the algebraic matroid \(M_X\) of the coordinate functions.

For \(B\subseteq[n]\), write
\[
 \pi_B:X\longrightarrow(\mathbb P^1)^B
\]
for coordinate projection. A \(d\)-element set \(B\) is a basis of \(M_X\) when \(r(B)=d\).

### 4. Approach map

The argument has four steps.

1. Interpret \(m_B\) as the generic degree of \(\pi_B\).
2. Use transcendence degree to identify the nonzero multidegrees with the bases of \(M_X\).
3. Use \(m_B=1\) to upgrade every basis projection from generically finite to birational.
4. Compare two adjacent birational basis charts. Their common \(d-1\) coordinates form a coefficient field, and the exchanged coordinates are two generators of the same one-variable rational function field. They must therefore differ by a Möbius transformation.

This gives an explicit compatibility law that is invisible if one records only the support of the multidegree.

### 7. Detailed proof, derivation, or heuristic

#### Lemma 7.1 (multidegree coefficient equals projection degree)

For a \(d\)-element set \(B\),
\[
 m_B=
 \begin{cases}
 [K:k(t_i:i\in B)],& r(B)=d,\\
 0,&r(B)<d.
 \end{cases}
\]

##### Proof

Intersecting with \(h_i\) for \(i\in B\) means imposing a general point condition in each of the factors indexed by \(B\). Thus the intersection is the fiber of \(\pi_B\) over a general point of \((\mathbb P^1)^B\).

If \(r(B)<d\), the image of \(\pi_B\) has dimension less than \(d\). It is a proper closed subset of the \(d\)-dimensional target, so a general fiber is empty and \(m_B=0\).

If \(r(B)=d\), the image closure has the same dimension as the target and hence is the whole target. The projection is dominant and generically finite. The scheme-theoretic length of its generic fiber is its function-field degree
\([K:k(t_i:i\in B)]\), and the same length is obtained over a general closed point. This is \(m_B\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma 7.2 (matroid support and birationality)

The function \(r\) is a matroid rank function of total rank \(d\), and the nonzero \(m_B\) are indexed exactly by its bases. If \(X\) is multiplicity-free, every basis projection is birational.

##### Proof

Algebraic independence of the elements \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\) defines an algebraic matroid. Equivalently, transcendence degree is normalized and monotone and satisfies submodularity. The coordinates generate \(K\), so the total rank is \(d\). Therefore a \(d\)-set \(B\) is a basis exactly when \(r(B)=d\).

Lemma 7.1 gives \(m_B>0\) exactly for these bases. Multiplicity-freeness then forces \(m_B=1\), so
\[
 [K:k(t_i:i\in B)]=1.
\]
The two fields are equal, which is the function-field criterion for \(\pi_B\) to be birational. Choosing one basis identifies \(K\) with the rational function field in its \(d\) coordinate functions, proving rationality of \(X\). \(\square\)

#### Lemma 7.3 (relative Möbius exchange)

For adjacent bases \(B=C\cup\{i\}\) and \(B'=C\cup\{j\}\), one has
\[
 t_j=\frac{a\,t_i+b}{c\,t_i+e}
\]
with coefficients in \(K_C=k(t_c:c\in C)\) and nonzero determinant.

##### Proof

Since \(C\) is an independent \((d-1)\)-set, \(K_C\) has transcendence degree \(d-1\). Lemma 7.2 applied to both bases gives
\[
 K=K_C(t_i)=K_C(t_j).
\]
After identifying \(K\) with \(K_C(T)\) by \(T\mapsto t_i\), the element \(t_j\) is another generator of the same one-variable rational function field. Thus substitution \(T\mapsto t_j\) is a \(K_C\)-automorphism of \(K_C(T)\). The classical identity
\[
 \operatorname{Aut}_{K_C}K_C(T)=\operatorname{PGL}_2(K_C)
\]
implies the displayed formula. Equivalently, if \(t_j=p(t_i)/q(t_i)\) is reduced, then
\([K_C(t_i):K_C(t_j)]=\max(\deg p,\deg q)=1\), so the rational function has degree one. This argument remains valid in positive characteristic. \(\square\)

#### Proof of the cycle statement

For every basis \(B\), let \(\iota_B:(\mathbb P^1)^B\dashrightarrow X\) be the rational inverse of \(\pi_B\). Define the oriented edge transition
\[
 \psi_{B,B'}=\pi_{B'}\circ\iota_B.
\]
Lemma 7.3 describes this map on an adjacent edge. Along a path,
\[
 \psi_{B_{m-1},B_m}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{B_0,B_1}
 =\pi_{B_m}\circ\iota_{B_0},
\]
because \(\iota_{B_\ell}\circ\pi_{B_\ell}\) is the identity rational map on \(X\). If \(B_m=B_0\), the right side is the identity. \(\square\)

#### Proof of the function-field reduction

Given \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\in F\), let \(X\) be the reduced closure of the image of the displayed rational map. A basis exists, and the basis-generation condition implies
\[
 k(X)=k(f_1,\ldots,f_n)=F,
\]
so the map is birational onto its image and \(\dim X=d\).

If \(B\) is a basis, then the \(f_i\) for \(i\in B\) are algebraically independent and generate \(F\). Hence the coordinate projection \(\pi_B\) is birational and its multidegree coefficient is one. If a \(d\)-set is not a basis, its coordinate image has dimension less than \(d\), and its coefficient is zero. Thus every coefficient is zero or one and the support is exactly the basis set of \(M\).

Conversely, start with \(X\), choose any basis \(B_0\), and use the birational projection \(\pi_{B_0}\) to identify
\[
 k(X)=k(t_i:i\in B_0)\cong k(z_1,\ldots,z_d).
\]
The definition of \(M_X\) gives the transcendence-degree conditions, and Lemma 7.2 gives the basis-generation conditions. \(\square\)

#### Worked family

Choose \(\lambda\in k\setminus\{0,1\}\), possible over every algebraically closed field, and set
\[
 f_1=u,\qquad f_2=v,\qquad f_3=u+v,\qquad f_4=u+\lambda v
\]
in \(k(u,v)\). Every pair is a linear coordinate system, so the image closure in \((\mathbb P^1)^4\) is multiplicity-free with support the uniform matroid \(U_{2,4}\).

For the adjacent bases \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{1,3\}\), the common field is \(k(f_1)=k(u)\), and
\[
 f_3=f_2+f_1.
\]
This is the relative Möbius map \(T\mapsto T+u\). Around the triangle
\[
 \{1,2\}\longrightarrow\{1,3\}\longrightarrow\{2,3\}
\longrightarrow\{1,2\},
\]
the transitions are
\[
 (u,v)\mapsto(u,u+v),\quad
 (u,w)\mapsto(w-u,w),\quad
 (v,w)\mapsto(w-v,v),
\]
and direct substitution gives the identity. Notice that the fixed coordinate, hence the coefficient field, changes along the cycle.

As a simple obstruction, the family \(\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\}\) cannot be the multidegree support of an integral subvariety of \((\mathbb P^1)^4\): it violates basis exchange. This is only a necessary obstruction extracted from the contextual theorem, not a classification of the separately stated deformation problem.

### 8. Verification and attempted falsification

Several possible failure modes were checked.

- **Chow-ring convention.** The coefficient of \(\prod_{i\notin B}h_i\) is obtained by intersecting with \(\prod_{i\in B}h_i\). Thus \(B\), not its complement, indexes the projection whose degree is \(m_B\).
- **Positive characteristic.** The proof uses the full function-field degree, including inseparable degree. Degree one still gives equality of fields. Also, a generator of \(K_C(T)\) has rational-function degree one in every characteristic, so the \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) conclusion is characteristic-free.
- **Changing coefficient fields.** A cycle of exchanges does not live in one fixed copy of \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\). The statement is instead made for composable birational maps between basis-coordinate spaces, where telescoping is rigorous.
- **Loops and constants.** A constant coordinate is a loop of \(M_X\) and belongs to no basis; none of the birational assertions uses it.
- **Dimension zero.** When \(d=0\), the only basis is empty and the exchange statement is vacuous. The theorem was stated for \(d\geq1\).
- **Support versus multiplicity.** Support alone is insufficient. For example, the image closure of
  \[
  z\longmapsto(z^2,z^3)\in(\mathbb P^1)^2
  \]
  has rank-one matroid support \(\{\{1\},\{2\}\}\), but its two projection degrees are \(2\) and \(3\), not \(1\). The Möbius law therefore correctly requires multiplicity-freeness, not merely matroidal support.
- **Worked example.** The determinants of all pairs among
  \((1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(1,\lambda)\) are nonzero exactly when
  \(\lambda\neq0,1\), so the claimed \(U_{2,4}\) support is correct in all characteristics.

No computer algebra or exhaustive computation was used. The only local checks were source lookup, text search, JSON inspection, and the displayed substitutions.
prior_report.result:
### 5. Main result

#### Theorem (birational basis charts and relative Möbius exchange)

Let \(X\subseteq(\mathbb P^1)^n\) be an integral \(d\)-dimensional multiplicity-free subvariety over an algebraically closed field \(k\).

1. For every \(d\)-element set \(B\),
   \[
   m_B>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\text{ is a basis of }M_X.
   \]
   If \(B\) is a basis, then \(m_B=1\), the projection
   \(\pi_B:X\to(\mathbb P^1)^B\) is birational, and
   \[
   k(X)=k(t_i:i\in B).
   \]
   In particular, \(X\) is rational.

2. Suppose \(B=C\cup\{i\}\) and \(B'=C\cup\{j\}\) are adjacent bases, so \(|C|=d-1\). Put \(K_C=k(t_c:c\in C)\). Then
   \[
   K_C(t_i)=k(X)=K_C(t_j),
   \]
   and there exist \(a,b,c,e\in K_C\) with \(ae-bc\neq0\) such that
   \[
   t_j=\frac{a\,t_i+b}{c\,t_i+e}.
   \]
   Equivalently, the birational transition from the \(B\)-projection chart to the \(B'\)-projection chart fixes the common coordinates and lies in
   \(\operatorname{PGL}_2(K_C)\) in the exchanged coordinate.

3. If
   \[
   B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_m=B_0
   \]
   is a cycle in the basis-exchange graph, the associated birational coordinate transitions compose to the identity on \((\mathbb P^1)^{B_0}\). The coefficient fields vary from edge to edge, so this is a cocycle identity in the groupoid of birational basis charts, not an assertion that all edge labels lie in one fixed \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\).

#### Corollary (exact function-field reduction)

Let \(M\) be a rank-\(d\) matroid on \([n]\), let \(F=k(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\), and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\in F\). The closure of the rational map
\[
 (\mathbb P^1)^d\dashrightarrow(\mathbb P^1)^n,\qquad
 z\longmapsto(f_1(z),\ldots,f_n(z)),
\]
is an integral multiplicity-free variety with multidegree support equal to the bases of \(M\) if the following two conditions hold:
\[
 \operatorname{trdeg}_k k(f_i:i\in I)=r_M(I)\quad\text{for every }I\subseteq[n],
\]
and
\[
 k(f_i:i\in B)=F\quad\text{for every basis }B\text{ of }M.
\]
Conversely, every integral multiplicity-free \(X\subseteq(\mathbb P^1)^n\) produces such data after one basis projection identifies \(k(X)\) with a rational function field.

This is a function-field reduction, not a combinatorial classification: deciding whether compatible functions exist remains a genuine realization problem.

### 6. Candidate novel contribution

**Candidate contribution.** The explicit relative-\(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) law for every adjacent matroid-basis exchange, together with its basis-graph cocycle and the exact rational-function realization formulation, appears to be a useful refinement of the known statement that multidegree support is a matroid.

**Scope.** It applies to integral multiplicity-free subvarieties of \((\mathbb P^1)^n\) over an algebraically closed field of any characteristic. It says nothing by itself about arbitrary flag manifolds, reducible general fibers, or the sufficiency of Cohen--Macaulayness for a Schubert union.

**Literature checked.** The original AIM PDF; Brion's 2003 paper; Ardila--Boocher's work on closures of linear spaces; Castillo--Cid-Ruiz--Li--Montaño--Zhang's multidegree-positivity theorem; Eur--Larson's 2026 paper; and targeted searches for combinations of “multiplicity-free,” “basis projection,” “birational,” “matroid,” and “PGL2/Möbius.” The matroid-support and linear-example ingredients are known. I did not locate this exact relative-Möbius/cocycle packaging, but an elementary observation can easily be implicit in other work.

**Novelty confidence: low.** The statement is concrete and proved below, but no claim of global priority is made.
prior_report.what_remains:
### 9. Limitations and unresolved gaps

1. AIM-ALGEBRAIC_GEOMETRY-0217 is context, not an open problem. The result above is an auxiliary structural consequence, not a solution to a question contained in this record.
2. The relative-\(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) law is necessary for a multiplicity-free realization, but the function-field criterion is not a purely combinatorial decision procedure.
3. No claim is made that every abstract assignment of edgewise Möbius transformations satisfying cycle identities comes from globally defined coordinate functions; descent and pole compatibility remain.
4. The argument is special to factors \(\mathbb P^1\). For higher-dimensional projective factors, adjacent basis changes are higher-dimensional birational transformations, not necessarily projective linear maps.
5. The literature search was targeted rather than exhaustive. The candidate contribution may already be implicit in work on algebraic matroids, multidegrees, or birational atlases.

### 10. Concrete next steps

1. Fix a matroid and formulate a precise moduli functor of compatible relative-\(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) edge transitions, quotienting by factorwise \(\operatorname{PGL}_2(k)\) coordinate changes.
2. Determine which cycle identities are independent, using a spanning tree of the basis graph, and add pole-divisor conditions needed for the local transitions to arise from a common function field.
3. Work out the rank-two case explicitly. There the coefficient fields are \(k(t_c)\), so zeros and poles of cross-ratios give computable compatibility invariants.
4. Compare these invariants with the affine-linear transitions in Ardila--Boocher's realizations. A nontrivial invariant would distinguish genuinely nonlinear multiplicity-free realizations from closures of linear spaces.

### References

1. American Institute of Mathematics, *Degenerations in Algebraic Geometry: Problem Session*, September 7, 2016, notes by Tony Feng. <https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/degenalggeomproblems.pdf>
2. Michel Brion, “Multiplicity-free subvarieties of flag varieties,” *Contemporary Mathematics* **331** (2003), 13--23. DOI: [10.1090/conm/331/05900](https://doi.org/10.1090/conm/331/05900); arXiv:math/0211028.
3. Federico Ardila and Adam Boocher, “The closure of a linear space in a product of lines,” *Journal of Algebraic Combinatorics* **43** (2016), 199--235. DOI: [10.1007/s10801-015-0634-x](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10801-015-0634-x); arXiv:1312.6874.
4. Federico Castillo, Yairon Cid-Ruiz, Binglin Li, Jonathan Montaño, and Naizhen Zhang, “When are multidegrees positive?”, *Advances in Mathematics* **374** (2020), 107382. DOI: [10.1016/j.aim.2020.107382](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aim.2020.107382); arXiv:2005.07808.
5. Christopher Eur and Matt Larson, “K-theoretic positivity for matroids,” *Algebraic Geometry* **13** (2026), no. 2, 241--265. DOI: [10.14231/AG-2026-008](https://doi.org/10.14231/AG-2026-008); arXiv:2311.11996.

prior_report.problem:
Section C.3 of the AIM list *Amoebas and tropical geometry* asks:

> A. How can examples of amoebas and tropical varieties be computed?
> B. Can one compute complement homology, and is there a Hermitian form whose
> signature equals the number of complement components?
> C. Which classical varieties are expansive, meaning that 0 lies in the
> amoeba?
> D. Develop the theory of smooth curves.
> E. What is the complexity of deciding resultant vanishing?
> F. When does Log(X) lie in a lower-dimensional subspace?
> G. What is the complexity of distance to the discriminantal variety?

The source PDF was checked directly. The isolated “17” is a page number, not
part of item C; item D follows after that page break. “Hermitean” is normalized
to “Hermitian,” “comple-ment” is dehyphenated, and “is 0 is in” is read as “is
0 in.” These are editorial repairs. For F, “subspace” is ambiguous; this report
treats affine subspaces, with linear subspaces as the zero-constant case.

This record is a research program rather than one proposition. The main result
below completely answers the qualitative part of F for irreducible very
affine varieties. The remaining items receive a concise status synthesis.

  amoeba complement is convex and has an order. Thus that complement is a
  disjoint union of contractible open sets: positive homology vanishes and
  the rank of \(H_0\) is the number of components. Henriques proves a
  higher-convexity result in higher codimension. The proposed Hermitian form is
  underspecified without its vector space and pairing; no canonical general
  form with the stated signature was found in the literature checked.

  \(X\cap(S^1)^n\ne\varnothing\). It is not intrinsic to an abstract variety:

  skeleta of curves. Abramovich--Caporaso--Payne identify the skeleton of the

### 3. Definitions and assumptions

Let
\[
T=(\mathbb C^*)^n,\qquad
\operatorname{Log}(z)=(\log|z_1|,\ldots,\log|z_n|),
\]
and let \(X\subset T\) be nonempty, irreducible, and closed algebraic. Its
amoeba is \(\mathcal A(X)=\operatorname{Log}(X)\).
For \(u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)\in\mathbb Z^n\), put
\(\chi^u(z)=z_1^{u_1}\cdots z_n^{u_n}\), and define
\[
\Lambda_X=\{u\in\mathbb Z^n:\chi^u|_X\text{ is constant}\}.
\]
Write the nonzero constant as \(\lambda_X(u)\). A lattice is saturated if
\(ku\) in the lattice, with \(k\ne0\), implies \(u\) is in it.

### 4. Approach map

First, an integral affine equality on the amoeba is shown equivalent to a
constant character by maximum modulus. Second, a real affine equality gives a
vanishing real linear combination of logarithmic differentials. Divisorial
valuations on a projective model turn its coefficient vector into the kernel
of an integer matrix; hence all real equations are generated by integral
ones. Finally, a saturated lattice of constant characters cuts out the
smallest subtorus coset containing \(X\). Laurent-ideal membership supplies a
finite certificate for each proposed character.

### 7. Detailed proof, derivation, or heuristic

Suppose \(\langle u,\operatorname{Log}z\rangle=c\) on \(X\). Then
\(|\chi^u(z)|=e^c\). If \(\dim X=0\), irreducibility makes \(X\) one point.
Otherwise \(X_{\rm reg}\) is connected, and the nowhere-vanishing holomorphic
function \(\chi^u\) has constant modulus there. Maximum modulus makes it
constant, and density extends the identity to \(X\). The converse follows by
taking absolute values.

Products and inverses prove that \(\Lambda_X\) is a group and \(\lambda_X\) a
homomorphism. If \(ku\in\Lambda_X\), the image of irreducible \(X\) under
\(\chi^u\) lies in a finite set of roots, hence is one point. Thus
\(u\in\Lambda_X\), proving saturation.

Now let \(a=(a_i)\in\mathbb R^n\) be normal to the affine hull. Then
\(F=\sum_i a_i\log|z_i|\) is constant. On \(X_{\rm reg}\), set
\[
\omega=\sum_i a_i\,\frac{dz_i}{z_i}.
\]
For every real tangent vector \(v\),
\(\operatorname{Re}\omega(v)=dF(v)=0\). Applying this to \(iv\) also gives
\(\operatorname{Im}\omega(v)=0\), so \(\omega=0\).

Choose a normal projective model \(\overline X\) of the function field. For
each prime divisor \(E\), the residue of \(\omega\) gives
\[
\sum_i a_i\operatorname{ord}_E(z_i)=0.                       \tag{7.1}
\]
Define the integer map
\[
D:\mathbb Z^n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Div}(\overline X),
\qquad D(u)=\operatorname{div}(z^u).
\]
Only finitely many divisors occur in the coordinate divisors, so (7.1) says
\(a\in\ker(D_{\mathbb R})\) for a finite integer matrix. Moreover,
\[
\ker D=\Lambda_X.
\]
Indeed, divisor zero means \(z^u\) is an invertible global regular function on
the complete normal variety \(\overline X\), hence a nonzero constant; the
converse is immediate. Integer linear algebra now gives
\[
\ker(D_{\mathbb R})=\Lambda_X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R.    \tag{7.2}
\]
Therefore every real normal is a real combination of integral constant-
character normals. Part 1 supplies the constants and proves (5.1).

A saturated sublattice of \(\mathbb Z^n\) is a direct summand. Extend
\(\lambda_X\) to the whole character lattice; that homomorphism is evaluation
at some \(t\in T\). Hence \(X\subset tH_{\Lambda_X}\). Any coset containing
\(X\) imposes constant characters, so its defining lattice lies in
\(\Lambda_X\), proving minimality. Finally (5.2) is precisely the coordinate-
ring statement that the class of \(z^u\) is scalar.

For a worked family, let
\[
X_\lambda=\{(x,y)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2:xy^2=\lambda\}.
\]
It is irreducible and isomorphic to \(\mathbb C^*\), with
\[
\Lambda_{X_\lambda}=\mathbb Z(1,2),\qquad
\mathcal A(X_\lambda)=\{(r,s):r+2s=\log|\lambda|\}.
\]
The phase of \(\lambda\) is present in the coset but invisible in its amoeba.

### 8. Verification and attempted falsification

- **Reducibility:** For
  \(X=(\{x=1\}\cup\{x=-1\})\times\mathbb C^*\), the amoeba is
  \(\{0\}\times\mathbb R\), but \(x\) is not constant on all of \(X\).
  Irreducibility is essential, or the result must be applied componentwise.
- **Irrational redundant equations:** For
  \(X=\{x=1,y=1\}\subset(\mathbb C^*)^3\), the amoeba is the \(w_3\)-axis and
  lies in \(\sqrt2w_1+w_2=0\). This equation is a real combination of the
  rational equations \(w_1=w_2=0\); the minimal flat is rational.
- **Dimension zero:** An irreducible zero-dimensional \(X\) is one point,
  \(\Lambda_X=\mathbb Z^n\), and (5.1) recovers its logarithm.
- **Saturation and phases:** Without saturation, character equations can cut
  out a disconnected union of cosets. The amoeba determines
  \(\log|\lambda_X(u)|\), not the phases.
- **Expansiveness:** The point \(\{1\}\subset\mathbb C^*\) is expansive,
  while its translate \(\{2\}\) is not. Hence C requires fixed coordinates.
- Negative exponents are valid in the torus; singularities are handled by the
  smooth locus and normal projective model.

No heavy computation was used.

### 5. Main result

#### Theorem 5.1 (affine hull and constant characters)

For nonempty irreducible \(X\subset(\mathbb C^*)^n\):

1. For \(u\in\mathbb Z^n\) and \(c\in\mathbb R\),
   \[
   \langle u,\operatorname{Log}z\rangle=c\quad(z\in X)
   \]
   holds if and only if \(\chi^u|_X=\lambda\in\mathbb C^*\) with
   \(\log|\lambda|=c\).
2. \(\Lambda_X\) is saturated and
   \(\lambda_X:\Lambda_X\to\mathbb C^*\) is a homomorphism.
3. The full affine hull is
   \[
   \operatorname{aff}_{\mathbb R}\mathcal A(X)=
   \{w:\langle u,w\rangle=\log|\lambda_X(u)|
   \text{ for every }u\in\Lambda_X\}.                       \tag{5.1}
   \]
   In particular the minimal affine hull is rational, and its codimension is
   \(\operatorname{rank}\Lambda_X\).
4. If
   \(H_{\Lambda_X}=\{z:\chi^u(z)=1\ \forall u\in\Lambda_X\}\),
   then \(H_{\Lambda_X}\) is connected and \(X\) lies in a translate
   \(tH_{\Lambda_X}\). This is the smallest torus coset containing \(X\).
5. For the Laurent ideal \(I(X)\),
   \[
   u\in\Lambda_X\iff
   z^u-\lambda\in I(X)\text{ for some }\lambda\in\mathbb C^*. \tag{5.2}
   \]

#### Corollary 5.2 (prescribed rational flat)

Let \(L\subset\mathbb Z^n\) be saturated and \(c:L\to\mathbb R\) additive.
Then
\[
\mathcal A(X)\subseteq\{w:\langle u,w\rangle=c(u)\ \forall u\in L\}
\]
if and only if a homomorphism \(\lambda:L\to\mathbb C^*\) exists with
\(\log|\lambda(u)|=c(u)\) and
\[
X\subseteq\{z:\chi^u(z)=\lambda(u)\ \forall u\in L\}.
\]
The set on the right is a subtorus translate. Thus \(\operatorname{Log}(X)\)
lies in a proper affine subspace exactly when a nontrivial character is
constant on \(X\).

### 6. Candidate novel contribution

**Candidate contribution.** Formula (5.1), especially the divisorial proof
that no genuinely irrational normal direction occurs, packages F as an exact
equality between the affine hull of an amoeba and the logarithm of the smallest
algebraic torus coset containing its variety. Equation (5.2) adds an elementary
Laurent-ideal certificate.

The ingredients are standard. Searches combining “amoeba affine span,”
“subtorus,” “contained in a hyperplane,” and “constant character” did not find
this exact formulation, but the search was not exhaustive. Novelty confidence
is therefore **low**; the result may be known folklore.

### 9. Limitations and unresolved gaps

The theorem does not give a complexity bound for computing all of
\(\Lambda_X\) from ideal generators. Reducible schemes require componentwise
lattices and compatibility data. This report neither constructs the Hermitian
form in B nor classifies every embedding in C. Item G remains ambiguous until
the norm, encoding, and output model are specified. The literature search was
targeted, so the novelty assessment is deliberately conservative.

### 10. Concrete next steps

1. Extract \(\Lambda_X\) algorithmically by combining tropical lineality
   spaces with exact binomial membership, and bound the bit complexity.
2. Extend the theorem to reducible schemes using component lattices and

3. Specify a finite-dimensional pairing for B before testing a signature
   formula.
4. Fix canonical torus charts for the families in C and test
   \(X\cap(S^1)^n\ne\varnothing\).
5. For G, fix rational input, Euclidean norm, and approximation tolerance,
   then compare ED-degree critical-point algorithms with numerical bounds.

prior_report.problem:
The exact AIM record is:

> **(11)** Prove Buch's weakened version of Knutson's false conjecture for the Schubert structure constants that arise in Schubert calculus on flag manifolds. The original conjecture turns out to be false for full flags, but seems to be OK for two-step flags \(V^a\subseteq V^b\subseteq \mathbb C^n\). A paper by Buch, Kresch, Tamvakis, and Yong (Duke Math. J. 122 (2004), 125--143) reduces \(q\)-Schubert calculus on Grassmannians to this two-step case.

The mathematical target can be recovered precisely. Let
\[
 X=\operatorname{Fl}(a,b;n)
 =\{(A,B):A\subset B\subset\mathbb C^n,
              \dim A=a,\ \dim B=b\}.
\]
A Schubert variety \(X_u\subset X\) is indexed by a **012-string** \(u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)\) having \(a\) zeros, \(b-a\) ones, and \(n-b\) twos. Its codimension is the inversion number
\[
 \ell(u)=\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ u_i>u_j\}.
\]
Knutson's two-step puzzle rule specifies eight small triangular pieces, allows rotations but not reflections, and requires adjacent edge labels to agree. If \(N_{u,v}^{w}\) denotes the number of such triangular puzzles with \(u,v\) on the left and right boundaries in clockwise direction and \(w\) on the bottom in counter-clockwise direction, the intended weakened conjecture is
\[
 [X_u][X_v]=\sum_w N_{u,v}^{w}[X_w]
 \qquad\text{in }H^*(\operatorname{Fl}(a,b;n);\mathbb Z). \tag{1}
\]
Equivalently, because the Poincaré dual of a 012-string is its reversal \(w^\vee\), the triple intersection
\(\int_X[X_u][X_v][X_z]\) is the number of puzzles whose three boundary strings \(u,v,z\) are read clockwise.

Two source repairs are necessary and are not silent rewrites.

1. “\(q\)-Schubert calculus” means **quantum** Schubert calculus here, not a free \(q\)-parameter in ordinary cohomology.
2. The bibliography in the AIM sentence is wrong for the asserted reduction. Buch--Kresch--Tamvakis--Yong, *Duke Math. J.* **122** (2004), 125--143, is **“Schubert polynomials and quiver formulas.”** The result reducing three-point genus-zero Gromov--Witten invariants on \(\operatorname{Gr}(k,n)\) to classical intersections on
   \[
   \operatorname{Fl}(k-d,k+d;n)
   \]
   is Buch--Kresch--Tamvakis, **“Gromov--Witten invariants on Grassmannians,”** *J. Amer. Math. Soc.* **16** (2003), 901--915. The mismatch is bibliographic, not an OCR corruption of the mathematical problem.
prior_report.status_literature:
The problem is solved. The following status was checked against primary sources and publication records through 12 August 2026.

- Knutson circulated the original puzzle conjecture for general type-A partial flag varieties in 1999 and found counterexamples to the unrestricted rule.
- Buch, Kresch, and Tamvakis proved in 2003 that every three-point, genus-zero Gromov--Witten invariant of a type-A Grassmannian equals a classical triple intersection on a two-step flag variety. This made the two-step restriction especially consequential.
- Coskun gave a different positive geometric Littlewood--Richardson rule for two-step flags in 2009, using Mondrian tableaux. It computed the constants but did not prove Knutson's specific puzzle rule.
- Buch proved an equivariant two-step puzzle formula in *Annals of Mathematics* in 2015. Its ordinary specialization already supplies the nonequivariant rule.
- Buch, Kresch, Purbhoo, and Tamvakis proved exactly (1) for every \(\operatorname{Fl}(a,b;n)\); their final paper appeared in *Journal of Algebraic Combinatorics* **44** (2016), 973--1007. Their proof constructs a mutation/gash-propagation bijection and proves that the puzzle product is the cohomology product.

The proof spine in the 2016 paper is useful to record. Define a bilinear operation \(\mu\) by the puzzle counts. The authors show:

1. multiplication by the identity string \(0^a1^{b-a}2^{n-b}\) is correct;
2. puzzle counts satisfy commutation identities matching the two Pieri families \(c_p(\mathbb C^n/B)\) and \(c_p(A^\vee)\);
3. those two families generate \(H^*(X;\mathbb Z)\), since \(X\) is a Grassmann bundle over a Grassmannian;
4. an elementary ring-recognition lemma then forces \(\mu(r,m)=rm\) for every pair of classes.

The hard step is the explicit bijection proving the Pieri commutation identities. Propagation paths can cross, so the proof uses simultaneous rather than sequential propagation and an audited list of local moves. This explains why the full proof is long even though its algebraic closure step is short.

The 2017 work of Knutson and Zinn-Justin places these and higher-step puzzle rules in an integrability framework and gives further \(K\)-theoretic rules. These extensions do not change the answer to the AIM record: its ordinary two-step statement is a theorem.

### 3. Definitions and assumptions

Let \(E_t=\langle e_t,e_{t+1},\ldots,e_n\rangle\). For a 012-string \(u\), define
\[
 A_u=\langle e_i:u_i=0\rangle,
 \qquad
 B_u=\langle e_i:u_i\le1\rangle.
\]
In the lower-triangular convention of Buch--Kresch--Purbhoo--Tamvakis, \(X_u\) is characterized by
\[
 \dim(A\cap E_t)\ge \#\{i\ge t:u_i=0\},
 \qquad
 \dim(B\cap E_t)\ge \#\{i\ge t:u_i\le1\} \tag{2}
\]
for every \(t\).

We will use the forgetful maps
\[
 \pi_b:X\to\operatorname{Gr}(b,n),\quad(A,B)\mapsto B,
 \qquad
 \pi_a:X\to\operatorname{Gr}(a,n),\quad(A,B)\mapsto A. \tag{3}
\]
Grassmannian Schubert varieties are indexed below by 02-strings: a word \(p\) with \(r\) zeros and \(n-r\) twos indexes a class in \(H^*(\operatorname{Gr}(r,n))\). Its Schubert condition is
\[
 \dim(V\cap E_t)\ge \#\{i\ge t:p_i=0\}. \tag{4}
\]
The product coefficients for these classes are the usual Littlewood--Richardson coefficients, after the standard word-to-partition dictionary.

### 4. Approach map

The work divided into four routes.

1. **Source reconstruction:** identify the conjecture as Knutson's eight-piece two-step puzzle rule and distinguish structure-constant and triple-intersection orientations.
2. **Bibliographic audit:** compare the cited Duke paper to the actual kernel-and-span reduction paper and explicitly repair the citation.
3. **Status route:** locate the 2015 equivariant theorem and 2016 ordinary theorem, and summarize the proof architecture without pretending to reproduce hundreds of local puzzle diagrams.
4. **Independent mathematical route:** exploit both forgetful maps (3). This gives an infinite family of exact two-step structure constants and a support-vanishing criterion that any puzzle implementation must satisfy.

### 7. Detailed proof, derivation, or heuristic

#### Proof of the \(b\)-projection assertion

Fix \(p\) and write its zero positions as \(z_1<\cdots<z_b\). The condition on \(B\) in (2) for \(u=\iota_b(p)\) is exactly (4), because
\[
 \{i:u_i\le1\}=\{i:p_i=0\}.
\]
It remains to show that the \(A\)-conditions in (2) impose nothing further on a pair \(A\subset B\) once \(B\in Y_p\).

Fix \(t\), and let
\[
 m=\#\{j:z_j<t\}.
\]
The Grassmannian condition gives \(\dim(B\cap E_t)\ge b-m\). Since \(A\subset B\), \(\dim A=a\), and \(\dim B=b\),
\[
 \dim(A\cap E_t)
 \ge \dim A+\dim(B\cap E_t)-\dim B
 \ge a-m. \tag{12}
\]
The number of zeros of \(\iota_b(p)\) in the suffix beginning at \(t\) is
\[
 \#\{j\le a:z_j\ge t\}=\max(a-m,0).
\]
Together with the trivial lower bound \(\dim(A\cap E_t)\ge0\), inequality (12) proves the required \(A\)-condition. Thus the inverse image in (6) is set-theoretically the indicated Schubert variety. Both are the same Schubert degeneracy locus; equivalently the forgetful map is smooth and the codimensions agree, so the cycle pullback also gives (6).

The codimension check is transparent: zeros and ones inserted at the zero positions occur in increasing order, so they have no mutual inversions; each earlier 2 creates exactly the same inversions with them as it did with the zeros of \(p\). Hence
\(\ell(\iota_b(p))=\ell(p)\).

#### Proof of the \(a\)-projection assertion

Now let the complement positions of the zeros of \(p\) be
\(y_1<\cdots<y_{n-a}\). For \(u=\iota_a(p)\), the \(A\)-condition in (2) is precisely the Grassmannian condition (4).

Fix \(t\). Let \(z\) be the number of zero positions before \(t\) and \(m\) the number of complement positions before \(t\). Then
\(z+m=t-1\). The required lower bound for \(B\cap E_t\) is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \#\{i\ge t:u_i\le1\}
 &= (a-z)+\max(b-a-m,0)\\
 &=\max(a-z,b-t+1). \tag{13}
 \end{aligned}
\]
For any \(B\supset A\), the inclusion gives
\[
 \dim(B\cap E_t)\ge\dim(A\cap E_t)\ge a-z,
\]
while the ambient dimension inequality in \(\mathbb C^n\) gives
\[
 \dim(B\cap E_t)\ge b+(n-t+1)-n=b-t+1.
\]
Taking the maximum yields exactly (13), so all \(B\)-conditions are automatic. The inserted ones precede all inserted twos and therefore create no internal inversions; every complement symbol remains larger than zero. Thus
\(\ell(\iota_a(p))=\ell(p)\), proving (8) also as an equality of classes.

#### Proof of the product and support formula

Pullback in cohomology is a ring homomorphism. Hence, for either projection,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 [X_{\iota_\epsilon(p)}][X_{\iota_\epsilon(q)}]
 &=\pi_\epsilon^*([Y_p])\,\pi_\epsilon^*([Y_q])\\
 &=\pi_\epsilon^*\left(\sum_r c_{p,q}^{r}[Y_r]\right)\\
 &=\sum_r c_{p,q}^{r}[X_{\iota_\epsilon(r)}].
 \end{aligned}
\]
The Schubert classes form a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis, so every coefficient outside the displayed support is zero. Finally, the 2016 puzzle theorem identifies these structure constants with the puzzle numbers, giving (10). \(\square\)

### 8. Verification and attempted falsification

- **Word convention:** the proof uses suffix spaces and lower-triangular orbits, exactly as in the 2016 paper. Switching to prefix spaces reverses the words and must not be done silently.
- **Poincaré duality:** the product-oriented bottom word is read counter-clockwise. For a triple intersection with all boundaries clockwise, the output word must be reversed.
- **Dimension bounds:** in the \(b\)-lift, \(m>a\) makes \(a-m<0\); the proof explicitly takes \(\max(a-m,0)\). In the \(a\)-lift, both the containment bound and the ambient-space bound are required to obtain the maximum in (13).
- **Codimension:** both lifts preserve inversion number, preventing hidden excess-codimension components in the pullback.
- **Degenerate cases:** if \(a=0\) or \(a=b\), one projection lift collapses to the usual Grassmannian indexing, as expected. The formulas remain meaningful after deleting an empty symbol block.
- **Worked example:** \(0212\) has one inversion, while \(0221\) and \(2012\) each have two, matching the degrees in (11).
- **Bibliography:** the title and DOI of the Duke paper were checked independently against the arXiv record and journal metadata; the JAMS paper itself states the kernel-and-span reduction to \(\operatorname{Fl}(k-d,k+d;n)\).
- **Novelty:** the projection theorem is not represented as a new solution of the puzzle conjecture. Its candidate novelty is only its explicit two-channel support-check formulation.

No heavy computation was used. The example and inversion checks are finite hand calculations.

### 5. Main result

The following proposition is elementary but gives a fully proved family inside the solved conjecture.

#### Proposition 5.1 (two projection lifts and Littlewood--Richardson collapse)

Let \(X=\operatorname{Fl}(a,b;n)\).

**The \(b\)-projection lift.** Let \(p\) be a 02-string with \(b\) zeros, occurring at positions
\(z_1<\cdots<z_b\). Define a 012-string \(\iota_b(p)\) by
\[
 (\iota_b(p))_{z_j}=
 \begin{cases}0,&j\le a,\\1,&j>a,\end{cases}
 \qquad
 (\iota_b(p))_i=2\quad\text{if }p_i=2. \tag{5}
\]
Then
\[
 \pi_b^{-1}(Y_p)=X_{\iota_b(p)},
 \qquad
 \pi_b^*[Y_p]=[X_{\iota_b(p)}], \tag{6}
\]
where \(Y_p\subset\operatorname{Gr}(b,n)\) is the Schubert variety indexed by \(p\).

**The \(a\)-projection lift.** Let \(p\) be a 02-string with \(a\) zeros. If its two-positions are
\(y_1<\cdots<y_{n-a}\), define
\[
 (\iota_a(p))_i=0\quad\text{if }p_i=0,
 \qquad
 (\iota_a(p))_{y_j}=
 \begin{cases}1,&j\le b-a,\\2,&j>b-a.
 \end{cases} \tag{7}
\]
Then
\[
 \pi_a^{-1}(Y_p)=X_{\iota_a(p)},
 \qquad
 \pi_a^*[Y_p]=[X_{\iota_a(p)}]. \tag{8}
\]

Consequently, for \(\epsilon\in\{a,b\}\),
\[
 [X_{\iota_\epsilon(p)}]\,[X_{\iota_\epsilon(q)}]
   =\sum_r c_{p,q}^{r}[X_{\iota_\epsilon(r)}], \tag{9}
\]
where \(c_{p,q}^{r}\) is the corresponding Grassmannian Littlewood--Richardson coefficient. Every coefficient of a Schubert class outside the image of \(\iota_\epsilon\) is zero.

By the proved puzzle theorem, (9) is also a puzzle enumeration statement:
\[
 N_{\iota_\epsilon(p),\iota_\epsilon(q)}^{w}
 =\begin{cases}
 c_{p,q}^{r},&w=\iota_\epsilon(r),\\
 0,&w\notin\operatorname{im}(\iota_\epsilon).
 \end{cases} \tag{10}
\]

#### Worked example

Take \(X=\operatorname{Fl}(1,2;4)\) and use \(\pi_b:X\to\operatorname{Gr}(2,4)\). In the Grassmannian,
\[
 [Y_{0202}]^2=[Y_{0220}]+[Y_{2002}],
\]
the familiar \(\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2+\sigma_{11}\). Formula (5) gives
\[
 \iota_b(0202)=0212,
 \quad \iota_b(0220)=0221,
 \quad \iota_b(2002)=2012.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \boxed{[X_{0212}]^2=[X_{0221}]+[X_{2012}].} \tag{11}
\]
Equivalently, exactly one product-oriented two-step puzzle occurs for each output \(0221\) and \(2012\), and none occurs for any other output word.

### 6. Candidate novel contribution

**Candidate contribution (explicit support lemma / implementation checksum; low novelty confidence).** Proposition 5.1 packages both forgetful projections as explicit scanning maps on 02-strings and deduces the support constraint (10): whenever both input boundaries are stable-order lifts from the same Grassmannian, every nonzero two-step puzzle output must be a stable-order lift, and its count is exactly an ordinary Littlewood--Richardson coefficient.

The underlying pullback fact is standard Schubert geometry, so no claim of deep novelty is made. The potentially useful contribution is the simultaneous two-projection formulation, the elementary suffix-dimension proof, and its conversion into an all-ranks puzzle checksum with forced zeros. I did not locate this exact diagnostic formulation in the AIM notes, the 2003 kernel-and-span paper, the 2015 equivariant puzzle paper, or the 2016 ordinary puzzle paper. Global novelty confidence is low; mathematical confidence is high.

### 9. Limitations and unresolved gaps

1. This report does not reproduce the 80 local propagation rules and hundreds of diagrams in the published proof; it cites the complete theorem accurately and explains its logical architecture.
2. Proposition 5.1 covers two pullback subrings, not arbitrary pairs of two-step Schubert classes.
3. The puzzle-piece list is referenced rather than redrawn; the eight oriented pieces and their rotations are fixed by the 2016 paper.
4. The main AIM problem concerns ordinary cohomology. Equivariant, \(K\)-theoretic, and higher-step variants require modified pieces or weights.
5. Candidate novelty confidence is low because parabolic pullback of Schubert classes is standard, even though the explicit implementation checksum was not found in the sources checked.

### 10. Concrete next steps

1. Use (10) as a regression suite for any program enumerating two-step puzzles: generate Grassmannian LR products, lift both inputs, and demand exact support and multiplicities.
2. Develop an analogous closed formula for **mixed** products \(\pi_a^*(\alpha)\pi_b^*(\beta)\). Unlike same-projection products, these probe genuinely two-step geometry.
3. Transport the two projection tests to Buch's equivariant rule; expected coefficients are factorial/equivariant Grassmannian LR polynomials and should obey the same support restriction.
4. For quantum Grassmannian applications, make the kernel-and-span conversion from a partition and degree \(d\) to its 012 boundary string explicit, then apply the verified two-step puzzle theorem.

## Classification result

For 6800007 / AMR-067-0007, the manuscript gives an explicit integral-cohomology classification of homotopies through totally real immersions of a fixed smooth real 3-manifold into the ordered complex full flag manifold. The stated scope includes nonorientable and noncompact sources without boundary, with ordinary homotopies and no properness requirement.

The indices are pairs of degree-two classes satisfying an orientation-Bockstein condition. Each fiber is a torsor for a degree-three cohomology group plus the cokernel of an explicit cup-product homomorphism. This computes the coupled monodromy action, rather than only restating the known h-principle or counting framings over a fixed map.

## Separate adversarial review

An independent topology reviewer returned PASS for the complete stated classification, with no mandatory correction. The audit specifically covers the formal h-principle, determinant constraint, integral virtual-Chern-class loop coordinates, stable range, complete quotient action, noncompact cellular argument, and genuine nonorientable torsion examples. All 1,595 independent exact assertions pass; the author's verification receipt was reproduced byte for byte.

Full review: `unsolved_math_prioritization/attempts/6800007/review/REVIEW.md`.
Frozen proof SHA-256: `501c9a536246ad06b29e16720c613bcb292c863857849f837bb0250c45a58050`.

## Attribution and limits

The h-principle, known three-sphere case, and general homogeneous-space obstruction-theory framework are credited. Historical novelty of the exact formula is unestablished. Independent AI review is not external peer review or formal verification. This does not classify embeddings, proper homotopies, source-diffeomorphism quotients, or the neighboring real-form uniformization question.

## Validation

- `python3 unsolved_math_prioritization/attempts/6800007/verify.py`
- `python3 unsolved_math_prioritization/attempts/6800007/review/independent_checks.py`
- SymPy 1.14.0; exact symbolic/integer calculations
- One substantive proof attempt; only this problem's attempt folder changes

Please retain this PR as an open draft for human review. No merge or release is requested.
